Ceva PWW

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: Three lines drawn across a triangle always meet at one spot, and a grid of smaller lines shows why.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Change the four counts, then switch on the grid pieces; press Reset diagram to start again.
Look for the math

Join three points on the sides of a triangle to the opposite corners. The three lines always pass through one point. Bogomolny's picture turns that fact into a counting game: the pieces of a grid tell you exactly how the three side ratios fit together.

Three lines, one meeting point

A line from a corner of a triangle to the opposite side is called a cevian. Here the cevians are AD, BE and CF, and they meet at K. Two counts set where E and F sit: AE:EC and AF:FB. The third point is placed at BD:DC = (AE·FB):(EC·AF), which is exactly the choice that makes the three lines meet. This is Ceva's theorem.

A grid of parallel lines

Draw lines through A, B and C parallel to the two cevians BE and CF. They make a parallelogram with corners A, Q, G, R. The fine grid cuts the side AQ into (AE+EC)·AF strips and the side AR into (AF+FB)·AE strips. The meeting point K lands at step AE·AF along both sides, so AK is the diagonal of a little grid square with AE·AF units on every side. The logic test checks this for all 10,000 choices of the four counts from 1 to 10.

Counting the pieces

Follow the grid lines that cross FB and let them turn at BE toward AD: they cut BD into FB·EA equal pieces. Starting from CE does the same for DC, giving CE·AF pieces. Because all the pieces are the same size in the grid, the article's claim follows:

BD/DC = FB·EA / (CE·AF).

Now multiply the three side ratios:

(AF/FB) · (BD/DC) · (CE/EA) = (AF/FB) · (FB·EA/(CE·AF)) · (CE/EA) = 1.

Everything cancels. The logic test measures the actual lengths on 10,000 different count settings and on thousands of dragged triangles; the identity holds every time. The idea is a proof by area and counting, not by measuring a particular drawing.

A note about the original applet

The applet's own description still says "A funny dissection that uses Fibonacci numbers" — a leftover from the Fibonacci dissection applet it was copied from. The page it appears on, and the explanation it links to, are about Ceva, so this port follows the Ceva picture. That explanation credits the grid proof to Professor William A. McWorter Jr.; the drawing and code here are written afresh.

Try AE = 10, EC = 1, AF = 1, FB = 10, switch on Show colors, and then drag a corner. The shapes change but the three ratios still multiply to 1.
